old: battered wallet
new: battered beggar's bag
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: The men were flung out into the sea; black-hulled and helpless, they were swept past the ship on the swell like sea-crows on the waves,
new: The men were flung out into the sea, and like sea-crows they were tossed on the waves around the black ship,
why: 'Black' belongs to the ship: κορώνῃσιν ἴκελοι περὶ νῆα μέλαιναν κύμασιν ἐμφορέοντο (14.308-9).

old: Instead the storm-winds have snatched him away, and no man knows where.
new: Instead the storm-winds have snatched him away without glory, and no man knows where.
why: Drops ἀκλειῶς (14.371), which answers the 'great glory for his son' just before.

old: led me here, to the steading of a wise man's door
new: led me here, to the farm of a man who knows what is right
why: Greek σταθμὸν ἀνδρὸς ἐπισταμένου (14.359); 'steading' is archaic and 'steading of a ... door' garbles the image.

old: I can hardly bring myself to say his name, stranger, he is not here, and yet he loved me and cared for me so well that I call him the master of my heart, far away as he is.
new: even though he is not here, stranger, I shrink from speaking his name, so dearly did he love me and care for me; I call him my dear master still, far away as he is.
why: Comma splices lost the sense; Greek 14.145-7: he shrinks from naming him even though absent, for he loved him; he calls him ἠθεῖον, dear master, though far away.

old: who above all the gods is angry at cruelty.
new: who is angered most of all by cruel deeds.
why: Read as 'angrier than the other gods'; Greek μάλιστα δὲ νεμεσσᾷ κακὰ ἔργα (14.284).

old: and a bright kilt.
new: and a bright war-belt.
why: Greek ζῶμα φαεινόν (14.482), a warrior's belt or loin-guard; 'kilt' brings a Scot to mind.

old: a man the swineherd had bought for himself while his master was away, with his own goods, telling neither his mistress nor old Laertes, paying for him out of the Taphians' hands.
new: a man the swineherd had bought from the Taphians with his own goods while his master was away, telling neither his mistress nor old Laertes.
why: 'Bought ... paying for him' said the same thing twice (14.449-52).

old: Eat, my strange friend,
new: Eat, my poor friend,
why: δαιμόνιε ξείνων (14.443); 'strange friend' reads as 'odd friend'.

old: hoping to wipe the name of Arceisius clean off the earth, out of Ithaca forever.
new: hoping to wipe the line of godlike Arceisius out of Ithaca and leave it without a name.
why: Greek ὅπως ἀπὸ φῦλον ὄληται νώνυμον ἐξ Ἰθάκης Ἀρκεισίου ἀντιθέοιο (14.181-2): the line perishing nameless; 'off the earth' and 'out of Ithaca' doubled.

old: spoke to him, his words flying:
new: spoke to him with winged words:
why: House formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα = 'winged words' (11 uses); 'his words flying' reads as a mistake.

old: of Kronos hung
new: of Cronus hung
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: of Kronos,
new: of Cronus,
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: 'Odysseus,' I whispered, 'royal son of Laertes, man of many turns —
new: 'Royal son of Laertes,' I whispered, 'Odysseus of the many schemes —
why: Repeated vocative διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν' Ὀδυσσεῦ: one rendering, as V seg-0014 ('Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many schemes'). πολυμήχανος is 'of many schemes'; 'many turns' is the edition's word for πολύτροπος (1.1).

old: in this steading
new: here at the farm
why: Policy: 'steading' is archaic; Eumaeus' σταθμός is 'the farm' (a fold for flocks).

old: Still, it is the cruel belly that drives men to all their wretched troubles, the man who knows want and grief and the long road.
new: Still, for the sake of the cursed belly men bear hard troubles — any man on whom wandering comes, and want, and grief.
why: The second clause hung from nothing. Greek 15.344-5: ἀλλ' ἕνεκ' οὐλομένης γαστρὸς κακὰ κήδε' ἔχουσιν ἀνέρες, ὅν τιν' ἵκηται ἄλη καὶ πῆμα καὶ ἄλγος.

old: a circuit through Hellas, or down through the Peloponnese,
new: a circuit through Hellas and the heart of Argos,
why: 'Peloponnese' is not in the text: ἀν' Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος (15.80), the same formula the edition renders 'Hellas and the heart of Argos' in Book IV.

old: comes in time to take a strange pleasure in his griefs
new: comes in time to take pleasure even in his griefs
why: 'Strange' is commentary; Greek μετὰ γάρ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι τέρπεται ἀνήρ (15.400) says it plainly.

old: with a black ship full of trinkets and trumpery.
new: with a black ship full of countless trinkets.
why: 'Trumpery' is leftover archaism; Greek μυρί' ἄγοντες ἀθύρματα (15.416).

old: "Strange, then — you must have been only a small child,
new: "Think of it — you were only a small child,
why: For ὢ πόποι (15.381), an exclamation of surprise and pity, 'Strange, then' reads as a non-sequitur.

old: When Dawn came with her rose-red fingers,
new: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared,
why: Repeated line ἦμος δ' ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς: one rendering everywhere, the edition's majority form ('When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared'). No 'again' or 'at last' in the Greek.

old: at the steading,
new: at the farm,
why: Policy: 'steading' is archaic; Eumaeus' σταθμός is 'the farm' (a fold for flocks).

old: of Kronos,
new: of Cronus,
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: the steading
new: the farm
why: Policy: 'steading' is archaic; Eumaeus' σταθμός is 'the farm' (a fold for flocks).

old: and eat and drink with his hands when the mood was on him.
new: and eat and drink with the servants in the house when he had a mind to.
why: Greek μετὰ δμώων ἐνὶ οἴκῳ πῖνε καὶ ἦσθ' (16.140-1): with the servants in the house; 'with his hands' reads as eating with his fingers.

old: "Stranger," he said, "you are changed — a moment ago, and now you are not the same man.
new: "Stranger," he said, "you are not the man you were a moment ago.
why: The syntax broke; Greek ἀλλοῖός μοι, ξεῖνε, φάνης νέον ἠὲ πάροιθεν (16.181).

old: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, born to many turns — now is the time.
new: "Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many schemes — now is the time.
why: Formula διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν' Ὀδυσσεῦ (16.167); merged two epithets and lost 'Zeus-born'. House rendering, as V seg-0014.

old: the man it falls to to win her.
new: the man who is fated to win her.
why: 'To to' trips aloud; Greek ὅς κε πλεῖστα πόροι καὶ μόρσιμος ἔλθοι (16.392).

old: He kissed his head and both his shining eyes and wept for joy.
new: He kissed his head and both his shining eyes and both his hands, and wept for joy.
why: Drops χεῖράς τ' ἀμφοτέρας (16.16).

old: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her smoothly:
new: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her:
why: No adverb in the Greek (16.434); 'smoothly' gives away the twist Homer saves for the end of the speech.

old: Servants lose half their worth the moment there is no master's hand over them; Zeus takes the better half of a man away
new: Servants stop doing honest work the moment their masters are no longer over them; for Zeus takes away half a man's worth
why: Two sayings were merged. Greek 17.320-3: servants no longer care to do their proper work when masters no longer rule them; Zeus takes away half a man's worth the day slavery takes him.

old: though he had never lived to get any use of him.
new: though he sailed before he had any joy of him.
why: 'Never lived to' says Odysseus died. Greek οὐδ' ἀπόνητο (17.293): he never had the joy of him, because he sailed first.

old: The rest I will leave to me and to heaven.
new: All the rest will be my concern, and the gods'.
why: Ungrammatical; Greek αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ τάδε πάντα καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μελήσει (17.601).

old: 'So these cowards would creep into a brave man's bed? A deer might as well lay her newborn fawns to sleep in a lion's den and wander off to graze the glens and the grassy hollows — and the lion, coming home to his lair, makes a bloody end of both. Just so will Odysseus make an end of these suitors. By Father Zeus, by Athena and Apollo — if Odysseus is still the man he was that day on Lesbos, when he stood up to wrestle Philomeleides and threw him so hard the whole army roared — if he came among these suitors still that man, they would find their wedding short and their death quick. As for what you ask me, I will not turn it aside or soften it: what the old man of the sea told me, all of it, I will tell you.
new: 'Shameless cowards — to think they'd lie down in the bed of a man like that! It's as if a deer had laid her newborn fawns to sleep in a lion's den and gone off to graze the wooded glens, and the lion came home to his lair and tore them apart, both of them, in a moment — that's how Odysseus will deal with those men, and bring their ugly fate on them. Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — if only the Odysseus who once stood up in lovely Lesbos and wrestled the son of Philomeleides and threw him down so hard that all the Greeks cheered — if only that Odysseus could meet these suitors now. Every one of them would find a quick death and a bitter wedding. But as for what you ask me and beg me to tell — I won't twist it aside or deceive you. Of all the old sea-god told me, I'll hide nothing.
why: Telemachus repeats Menelaus word for word (17.124-41 = 4.333-50); the edition rendered it twice, differently, and garbled the formula 'swift death and bitter wedding' ('wedding short'). Repeat IV seg-0026 as patched.

old: did not so much as rock him on his feet.
new: did not so much as stagger him.
why: 'Rock' twice in one sentence.

old: one of the high-born young men spoke up:
new: one of the arrogant young men spoke up:
why: Greek ὑπερηνορεόντων (17.481), overbearing; 'high-born' softens it.

old: to eat him out of house.
new: to eat him out of house and home.
why: The idiom is cut short (Greek ὃς τρύξει αὐτόν, 17.387).

old: their own corn and wine
new: their own grain and wine
why: An American reader takes 'corn' for maize; Greek σῖτος (17.533).

old: to look after the property — yours and what is mine.
new: to look after things there — your living and mine.
why: Awkward; Greek κεῖνα φυλάξων, σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν βίοτον (17.597).

old: God forbid.
new: Heaven forbid.
why: A monotheist idiom; Greek μὴ τοῦτο θεὸς τελέσειε (17.399), 'may a god not bring it about'.

old: Old Euryclea,
new: Old Eurycleia,
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: the steading
new: the farm
why: Policy: 'steading' is archaic; Eumaeus' σταθμός is 'the farm' (a fold for flocks).

old: torn old wallet
new: torn old beggar's bag
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: old wallet at
new: old bag at
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: his wallet with
new: his bag with
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: full wallet at
new: full bag at
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: his wallet;
new: his bag;
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: for anyone who sent him — a man's twist on Iris, the runner of the gods.
new: for anyone who sent him.
why: The clause after the dash explains the joke; Homer gives only the reason (18.6-7 οὕνεκ' ἀπαγγέλλεσκε κιών). If wanted, the Iris note belongs in the enrichment sidecar.

old: who used to go cadging all over the town
new: who used to beg his way all over the town
why: 'Cadging' is British slang many readers will not know; Greek πτωχεύεσκ' (18.2).

old: I will make you pay, mouthing off like that in front of everyone,
new: I will make you pay for talking like that in front of everyone,
why: Current slang that dates fast, in Eurymachus' mouth; Greek ἦ τάχα τοι δώσω κακόν, οἷ' ἀγορεύεις (18.389).

old: will fall to a miserable woman whose happiness Zeus has stripped away.
new: will fall on me, cursed as I am, whose happiness Zeus has stripped away.
why: The shift to third person leaves the reader wondering who is meant; Greek οὐλομένης ἐμέθεν, τῆς τε Ζεὺς ὄλβον ἀπηύρα (18.273).

old: But I do take in everything now,
new: But I see and understand everything now,
why: Stiff; Greek αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ θυμῷ νοέω καὶ οἶδα ἕκαστα (18.228).

old: torn old wallet
new: torn old beggar's bag
why: Policy: 'wallet' in its old sense (πήρη, a beggar's bag) now means a billfold; 'beggar's bag' at first mention, then 'bag'.

old: Many another likely tale he told her, and Penelope wept
new: So he went on, telling lie after lie that sounded like the truth; and Penelope wept
why: The famous line ἴσκε ψεύδεα πολλὰ λέγων ἐτύμοισιν ὁμοῖα (19.203) was flattened: he made his many lies seem like the truth.

old: for steel within a man's reach has a way of drawing his hand to it.
new: for the iron itself draws a man on.
why: Same Greek line as 16.294 (αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος, 19.13), rendered 'for the iron itself draws a man on' in XVI seg-0024; Homer repeats it, so the edition does. 'Steel' is also anachronistic.

old: that come up out of the water to eat the soaked grain,
new: that eat their grain soaked in water,
why: Greek πυρὸν ἔδουσιν ἐξ ὕδατος (19.536-7): they eat wheat out of water; they do not come up out of a pond.

old: and the East and South winds breathe upon it,
new: and the East Wind thaws it,
why: The South wind is added; Greek ἥν τ' Εὖρος κατέτηξεν, ἐπὴν Ζέφυρος καταχεύῃ (19.206).

old: 'Young men, my suitors — since noble Odysseus is dead, hold back from this marriage, eager as you are, until I have finished this cloth, so the threads will not be wasted. It is a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day death takes him down in its long sleep — for I would not have the women of this land reproach me, if a man who won so much should lie without a shroud.'
new: 'Young men, my suitors, since noble Odysseus is dead, you are eager for the wedding, I know; but wait, be patient, until I finish this cloth — I don't want all my spinning to go to waste — a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day that death's long grief comes and takes him. The women of Ithaca would never forgive me if a man who won so much should lie in his grave without a shroud.'
why: Penelope's shroud speech is the same Greek at 2.96-102, 19.139-47 and 24.131-7; the edition gave three versions ('long grief', 'long sleep', 'long sorrow'). All three now repeat Book II seg-0007.

old: Let this be the last supper they ever eat.
new: Let this be the last meal they ever eat.
why: 'Last supper' brings the Gospels into a pagan poem; Greek ὕστατα καὶ πύματα δειπνήσειαν (20.119).

old: God forbid I should.
new: Heaven forbid I should.
why: Monotheist idiom; Greek μὴ τοῦτο θεὸς τελέσειεν (20.344).

old: This is no public house.
new: This house is not common property.
why: Many readers hear 'pub'; Greek οὔ τοι δήμιός ἐστιν ὅδ' οἶκος (20.264-5), a house belonging to the people.

old: to load the cattle and go off to some other country,
new: to drive the cattle off to some other country,
why: You do not 'load' cattle to drive them overland; Greek ἄλλων δῆμον ἱκέσθαι αὐτῇσιν βόεσσιν (20.219).

old: to Euryclea:
new: to Eurycleia:
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

new: wise Eurycleia answered.
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: And Euryclea,
new: And Eurycleia,
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: "It is here. The man himself. It is I.
new: "He is here — the man himself. It is I.
why: 'It is here' has no referent, at the moment of revelation; Greek ἔνδον μὲν δὴ ὅδ' αὐτὸς ἐγώ (21.207).

old: So he spoke, and his words stayed unwinged on her lips: she went and bolted
new: So he spoke, and she answered not a word, but went and bolted
why: Pronouns mixed ('his words ... on her lips'). Greek τῇ δ' ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος (21.386): her word was wingless — she made no reply and obeyed.

old: But Odysseus, the man of many turns, once he had lifted the great bow and looked it over end to end — easily, as a man skilled in the lyre and in song slips a new string onto its peg,
new: But Odysseus, the man of many turns, lifted the great bow and looked it over end to end. And as a man skilled in the lyre and in song easily slips a new string onto its peg,
why: The opening subject was left hanging and Odysseus named twice in the climactic sentence (21.404-9).

old: girt his sharp sword about him,
new: slung his sharp sword over his shoulder,
why: 'Girt' is leftover archaism; Greek ἀμφὶ δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ βάλετ' (21.431). Same wording as XX seg-0010.

old: not in all Achaean land
new: not in all the land of the Greeks
why: Policy: Ἀχαιοί/Ἀργεῖοι/Δαναοί and their adjectives are 'Greeks'/'Greek' (107 uses), except in ethnic lists (XIX seg-0015 keeps 'Achaeans' beside Cretans and Dorians).

old: some other fine Achaean woman
new: some other fine Greek woman
why: Policy: Ἀχαιοί/Ἀργεῖοι/Δαναοί and their adjectives are 'Greeks'/'Greek' (107 uses), except in ethnic lists (XIX seg-0015 keeps 'Achaeans' beside Cretans and Dorians).

old: other Achaean women enough
new: other Greek women enough
why: Policy: Ἀχαιοί/Ἀργεῖοι/Δαναοί and their adjectives are 'Greeks'/'Greek' (107 uses), except in ethnic lists (XIX seg-0015 keeps 'Achaeans' beside Cretans and Dorians).

old: great-hearted Peirithous,
new: great-hearted Pirithous,
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: under Peirithous's
new: under Pirithous's
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: some lesser Achaean
new: some lesser man among the Greeks
why: Policy: Ἀχαιοί/Ἀργεῖοι/Δαναοί and their adjectives are 'Greeks'/'Greek' (107 uses), except in ethnic lists (XIX seg-0015 keeps 'Achaeans' beside Cretans and Dorians).

old: no Achaean has more right
new: no Greek has more right
why: Policy: Ἀχαιοί/Ἀργεῖοι/Δαναοί and their adjectives are 'Greeks'/'Greek' (107 uses), except in ethnic lists (XIX seg-0015 keeps 'Achaeans' beside Cretans and Dorians).

old: crooked-counseling Kronos had
new: crooked-counseling Cronus had
why: House name list: the familiar Latinized English spelling of each Greek name, the form the edition already uses for nearly every name (Telemachus, Alcinous, Antinous 52x) and the form of the Lectio Iliad (Cronus). One spelling per person.

old: Odysseus posted Philoetius to guard it, since only one man could come at it at a time.
new: Odysseus posted the noble swineherd to guard it, standing close by, since there was only one way in.
why: Greek 22.129-30: Ὀδυσεὺς φράζεσθαι ἀνώγει δῖον ὑφορβόν ... οἴη δ' ἔχεν ἔμβασις αὐτῆς. Philoetius is Butler's slip, copied here.

old: And as hawks with hooked beaks
new: And as vultures with hooked beaks
why: Greek αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες (22.302): vultures, not hawks.

old: and the hawks fall on them and kill, and there is no help and no escape —
new: and the vultures fall on them and kill, and there is no help and no escape, and men look on and delight in the chase —
why: Drops the last cruel touch of the simile, χαίρουσι δέ τ' ἀνέρες ἄγρῃ (22.306).

old: And the swineherd Eumaeus stood over him and jeered:
new: And you, Eumaeus, swineherd, stood over him and jeered:
why: Homer addresses Eumaeus here (τὸν δ' ἐπικερτομέων προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα, 22.194); the edition keeps the device everywhere else.

old: to card the wool and carry the load of the household.
new: to card the wool and to bear their lot as slaves.
why: Greek δουλοσύνης ἀνέχεσθαι (22.423); softening it blurs what the hanging means.

old: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, there he goes
new: "Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many schemes, there he goes
why: Repeated vocative διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν' Ὀδυσσεῦ: one rendering, as V seg-0014 ('Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many schemes'). πολυμήχανος is 'of many schemes'; 'many turns' is the edition's word for πολύτροπος (1.1).

old: There are so many cruel and scheming men in the world. But now you have spoken the secret of our bed, the sign no living soul has seen but you and I, and the one maid my father gave me when I came here,
new: There are so many cruel and scheming men in the world. Helen of Argos herself, daughter of Zeus, would never have lain in love with a man from a foreign land if she had known that the warlike sons of the Greeks would bring her home again to her own country. It was a god who drove her to that shameful act; she had not taken to heart, before, the blindness that was the start of sorrow for us too. But now you have told the sure signs of our bed, which no living soul has seen but you and I, and Actoris, the maid my father gave me when I came here,
why: 23.218-24 (the Helen lines) were dropped without note: οὐδέ κεν Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα ... τὴν δ' ἄτην οὐ πρόσθεν ἑῷ ἐγκάτθετο θυμῷ λυγρήν, ἐξ ἧς πρῶτα καὶ ἡμέας ἵκετο πένθος. Doubted by ancient critics but in the standard text and in Butler; restored. Also restores the maid's name Ἀκτορίς (23.228) and 'signs' for σήματα (23.225).

old: There is a secret built into it,
new: There is a great sign built into it,
why: Greek μέγα σῆμα τέτυκται (23.188): 'sign', the word of 23.110 and the book's title; 'secret' breaks the thread.

old: That is my secret.
new: That is the sign I give you.
why: Greek οὕτω τοι τόδε σῆμα πιφαύσκομαι (23.202).

old: who destroyed his ships and his men, every one but himself;
new: who destroyed his ships and their crews, all of them — only Odysseus escaped, in his black ship;
why: Greek Ὀδυσσεὺς δ' οἶος ὑπέκφυγε νηῒ μελαίνῃ (23.320): he escaped with his black ship.

new: 'Young men, my suitors, since noble Odysseus is dead, you are eager for the wedding, I know; but wait, be patient, until I finish this cloth — I don't want all my spinning to go to waste — a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day that death's long grief comes and takes him. The women of Ithaca would never forgive me if a man who won so much should lie in his grave without a shroud.'
why: Same Greek as 2.96-102 and 19.139-47 (24.131-7); repeat Book II seg-0007 word for word.
